sections.title: The definite article: all the forms

body.p: Greek has one definite article, declined for three genders, two numbers and three cases. There is no vocative form: when you call someone, the article drops (see part 9).

Notice the patterns that make it easier: the neuter has the same form in the nominative and accusative (το, τα), the genitive plural is **των** for every gender, and masculine and feminine share **οι** in the nominative plural.

ex.el: ο δάσκαλος, τον δάσκαλο, του δασκάλου
η μητέρα, τη μητέρα, της μητέρας
το παιδί, το παιδί, του παιδιού
οι δάσκαλοι, τους δασκάλους, των δασκάλων
οι μητέρες, τις μητέρες, των μητέρων
τα παιδιά, τα παιδιά, των παιδιών

body.tip: The nominative singular forms **ο** and **η** carry no accent, and neither do the plural forms. Do not confuse the article **η** with the conjunction **ή** "or", which is accented: η μητέρα ή ο πατέρας "the mother or the father".

check.q: Which form goes with "the women" as the object of a verb (accusative plural feminine)?
check.why: Feminine accusative plural is τις. Τους is masculine.

check.q: Which article is the same for all three genders?
check.why: The genitive plural των serves masculine, feminine and neuter alike.

body.p: The masculine accusative **τον** always keeps its ν. The feminine accusative **τη(ν)** keeps it only before a vowel or before a consonant that is a stop or a double consonant: **κ, π, τ, ξ, ψ**, and the combinations **γκ, μπ, ντ, τσ, τζ**. Before every other consonant it is normally dropped.

Feminine

την κόρη, την πόρτα, την τάξη

body.p: The same rule applies to the weak pronoun **τη(ν)** "her", to the negative **δε(ν)** and **μη(ν)**, and to **στη(ν)** (σε + article). The masculine **τον** and **στον** keep the ν everywhere.

ex.en: I saw Anna at the bus stop.

ex.el: Δεν την ξέρω, αλλά τη θυμάμαι.
ex.en: I don't know her, but I remember her.

ex.el: Θα σε δω τη Δευτέρα ή την Τρίτη.
ex.en: I'll see you on Monday or Tuesday.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Πέρασα ___ γέφυρα.
check.why: Γ is not on the list of sounds that keep the ν, so τη γέφυρα.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Άνοιξε ___ πόρτα.
check.why: Π keeps the ν: την πόρτα.

body.p: The indefinite article is the numeral "one" used as an article. It exists only in the singular.

ex.el: Έχω έναν αδελφό και μια αδελφή.
ex.en: I have a brother and a sister.
I'd like a (bottle of) water, please.
The house of a friend of mine.

body.p: The masculine accusative **έναν** normally keeps its ν, especially before a vowel. The feminine accusative **μιαν** is mostly written **μια**; the ν appears in careful or literary style before a vowel: μιαν άλλη φορά "another time".
**μια** is pronounced as one syllable [mɲa]. When you stress the number "one" rather than "a", it is often written **μία** in two syllables: Έμεινα μόνο μία εβδομάδα "I stayed only one week".
There is no plural indefinite article. For "some" Greek uses no article at all, or **κάτι**, **κάποιοι/κάποιες/κάποια** or **μερικοί/μερικές/μερικά** (see part 7).

check.q: How do you say "a cup" (κούπα, feminine) as an object: Θέλω ___ κούπα.
check.why: Feminine accusative is μια (μιαν only in careful style before a vowel).

sections.title: Fusing with σε: στο, στη, στον

body.p: The preposition **σε** "in, at, to, on" merges with the definite article into a single word. This happens every time; σε το is never written.

ex.el: Πάω στον φούρνο, στη λαϊκή και στο περίπτερο.
ex.en: I'm going to the bakery, the street market and the kiosk.
We live in Athens, in Ampelokipi.

ex.el: Τα κλειδιά είναι στα παπούτσια σου.
ex.en: The keys are in your shoes.

body.p: The genitive article never combines with σε, because σε takes the accusative. The prepositions **από**, **για**, **με** do not fuse in writing, though in speech από το is often heard as απ' το: απ' το σπίτι "from the house".

Many noun endings are ambiguous. **-ες** can be feminine nominative plural or accusative plural; **-α** can be nominative or accusative; masculine **-ας** nouns end in **-α** in the accusative and genitive singular. The article resolves this at once:
This is why word order in Greek is so free: the article tells you who did what to whom, so the subject does not have to come first.

ex.el: Τον Γιάννη τον είδε η Μαρία.
ex.en: Maria saw Giannis. (The object comes first; τον and η keep the roles clear.)

ex.el: Τη Μαρία την είδε ο Γιάννης.

body.tip: When you learn a new noun, learn it with its article: **η λέξη**, **το κείμενο**, **ο χάρτης**. The article is the gender label, and gender decides every other form.

check.q: In Τις καρέκλες τις έφερε ο Νίκος, who brought what?
check.why: Τις is accusative (object), ο is nominative (subject).

sections.title: The article with names of people and places

body.p: Greek puts the definite article before proper names, both of people and of places. Leaving it out sounds abrupt or foreign.

ex.el: Η Γαλλία, η Ιταλία και η Ισπανία.

body.p: Titles also take the article: **ο κύριος**, **η κυρία**, **η δεσποινίς**, **ο γιατρός**, **ο καθηγητής**: Μίλησα με την κυρία Αντωνίου "I spoke with Mrs Antoniou".
The article drops when you address the person (vocative), when the name is a label or title, and in some fixed phrases:

ex.en: My name is Eleni. (The name is a predicate label, so no article.)

body.p: Most names of cities and islands are feminine, partly because the ancient words for "city" (πόλις) and "island" (νήσος) were feminine: **η Αθήνα, η Πάτρα, η Κέρκυρα, η Κρήτη, η Ρόδος, η Σαντορίνη**. But many are not, so learn each with its article: **ο Βόλος, ο Πειραιάς, το Ηράκλειο, το Άργος, το Ναύπλιο, τα Χανιά, τα Ιωάννινα, οι Σέρρες**.

check.q: Which is natural Greek for "I know Maria"?
check.why: Names take the article: τη Μαρία. (Ξέρω μια Μαρία means "I know a Maria", someone called Maria.)

check.q: Fill in: Πάμε ___ Χανιά το καλοκαίρι.
check.why: Τα Χανιά is neuter plural, so στα Χανιά.

sections.el: Το άρθρο όπου τα αγγλικά δεν βάζουν
sections.title: Where Greek has "the" and English has nothing

body.p: Greek uses the definite article whenever a noun refers to a whole category, a substance, an abstract idea, or a known activity. English often uses a bare noun in these cases.

list: **Whole classes in the plural:** Αγαπάω τα σκυλιά "I love dogs". Οι Έλληνες πίνουν πολύ καφέ "Greeks drink a lot of coffee".
**Abstract nouns:** Η ζωή είναι ωραία "Life is beautiful". Η δημοκρατία γεννήθηκε στην Αθήνα "Democracy was born in Athens".
**Substances and materials:** Ο χρυσός είναι ακριβός "Gold is expensive". Το νερό βράζει στους εκατό βαθμούς "Water boils at a hundred degrees".

**Languages, sports, school subjects:** Μαθαίνω τα ελληνικά "I'm learning Greek". Μου αρέσει το ποδόσφαιρο "I like football". Η ιστορία ήταν το αγαπημένο μου μάθημα "History was my favourite subject".
**Meals and parts of the day:** Τι τρώμε για το μεσημεριανό; "What are we having for lunch?" Το πρωί πίνω τσάι "In the morning I drink tea".
**Body parts, with a possessive or without:** Πονάει το κεφάλι μου "My head hurts". Σήκωσε το χέρι "Raise your hand".

body.p: With **μιλάω** "speak" a language can also appear without the article when you mean "speak (some) Greek" as an ability: Μιλάς ελληνικά; "Do you speak Greek?" Both Μιλάς ελληνικά; and Μιλάς τα ελληνικά; are heard; the bare form is more common in this question.

check.q: Translate "I don't like coffee" naturally:
check.why: A substance or category in general takes the article: ο καφές.

sections.title: Days, months, seasons, dates and rates

body.p: Time expressions take the article. In the nominative the article names the day or month; in the **accusative** it means "on" or "in", with no preposition.

ex.el: Η Κυριακή είναι η αγαπημένη μου μέρα.

ex.en: In summer we stay on the island.
(S)he left on the fifteenth of May.

body.p: Clock times and dates use **στις** (σε + τις, because ώρες and μέρες of the month are understood): στις τρεις "at three", στις είκοσι πέντε Μαρτίου "on the 25th of March". One o'clock uses **στη μία**.
**Rates** use the accusative article where English says "a" or "per":

ex.en: I pay four hundred euros a month.

ex.el: Πήγαινε με εκατό χιλιόμετρα την ώρα.
ex.en: (S)he was doing a hundred kilometres an hour.

ex.el: Τρεις φορές τη μέρα, μετά το φαγητό.
ex.en: Three times a day, after meals.

check.q: "In winter it snows" is:
check.why: The bare accusative with the article means "in": τον χειμώνα.

check.q: "Five euros a kilo":
check.why: Rates use the definite article: το κιλό.

sections.title: The article with possessives and demonstratives

body.p: **Possessives.** Greek says "the house my", with the article: **το σπίτι μου**. Without the article, or with the indefinite one, the phrase means "a ... of mine".

**Demonstratives.** **Αυτός**, **εκείνος** and **τούτος** before a noun always need the article: **αυτό το βιβλίο** "this book", **εκείνη η μέρα** "that day". Leaving the article out is a typical learner error.

ex.el: Το βιβλίο αυτό το διάβασα δύο φορές.
ex.en: This book I have read twice. (The demonstrative can follow the noun, still with the article.)

body.p: **Όλος** "all, the whole" also takes the article: **όλη η μέρα** "all day", **όλοι οι φίλοι μου** "all my friends", **όλο το βράδυ** "all evening". **Ολόκληρος** "whole" takes it too, though it can drop in phrases of duration: ολόκληρο το καλοκαίρι "the whole summer", but ολόκληρες ώρες "for hours on end".

check.q: "This street" is:
check.why: Demonstrative + article + noun: αυτή η οδός. (Η αυτή οδός would mean "the same street" in formal Greek.)

sections.el: Η κλητική και η απουσία άρθρου
sections.title: No article in the vocative

body.p: The vocative case never takes an article. If you add ο or η when calling someone, it sounds like you are talking about them, not to them.
In speech the particle **ρε** or **βρε** may come before the vocative (familiar): Βρε Νίκο, τι κάνεις; See the document on particles.

sections.title: Where Greek has no article and English has "a" or "some"

body.p: Greek often leaves the noun bare where English needs "a", "any" or "some".
**1. After είμαι, γίνομαι and similar verbs, for professions, nationalities and roles.**
Adding **ένας/μια** here is possible only when you describe someone by a quality: Είναι ένας πολύ καλός γιατρός "He is a very good doctor".
**2. After σαν "like" and ως "as".**
**3. An object whose identity does not matter, especially with έχω, φοράω, ψάχνω, αγοράζω, κάνω, and in questions, negatives and conditions.**

ex.en: I'm looking for a house in the centre.
If you find a taxi, call me.

body.p: Using **ένα** here would stress "one": Έχω ένα αυτοκίνητο, όχι δύο "I have one car, not two".
**4. Unspecified quantities ("some").**

**5. Many fixed phrases with prepositions:** με λεωφορείο "by bus", με τα πόδια "on foot" (here with article), σε κίνδυνο "in danger", από κοντά "up close", για πλάκα "for fun", στο σπίτι "at home" (with article), με χαρά "gladly".

check.q: "Do you have children?" is most natural as:
check.why: A question about whether something exists keeps the noun bare: Έχετε παιδιά;

check.q: "She is a teacher":
check.why: Professions after είμαι take no article. (Είναι η δασκάλα means "She is the teacher", a specific one.)

body.p: The article combines with **ένας** and **άλλος** in reciprocal and distributive phrases.

ex.en: They help each other. (literally: the one helps the other)

ex.el: Οι μεν μιλούσαν, οι δε άκουγαν.
ex.en: Some were talking, the others listening. (formal)
We'll talk about the rest tomorrow.

body.p: When the two people differ in gender, the masculine is used for the mixed pair: ο ένας τον άλλο. If both are women: η μία την άλλη.

**ο ίδιος** means "the same" or "himself": ο ίδιος άνθρωπος "the same person", ο ίδιος το είπε "he said it himself". Without the article ίδιος means "similar, identical": Είναι ίδιος ο πατέρας του "He is just like his father".
In a list of nouns, the article is repeated before each one, especially when they differ in gender or number.

ex.el: Ο πατέρας, η μητέρα και τα παιδιά.
Πήρα το διαβατήριο, την ταυτότητα και τα εισιτήρια.
ex.en: I took the passport, the ID card and the tickets.

body.p: **Adjective after the noun.** An adjective can follow its noun only if the article is repeated before the adjective as well. This gives emphasis or contrast, and is more literary.

ex.en: the new house (as opposed to the old one)

ex.el: Θέλω το φόρεμα το κόκκινο, όχι το μπλε.
ex.en: I want the red dress, not the blue one.

body.p: The normal order is **article + adjective + noun**: **το καινούριο σπίτι**.
**The article without a noun.** The noun can be left out when it is clear from context; the article and adjective then stand alone, like English "the red one".

ex.en: Which dress do you want? The red one.
The best is yet to come.

check.q: "The red one" (talking about a car, το αυτοκίνητο) is:
check.why: The article plus adjective stands in for the noun: το κόκκινο.

sections.title: The neuter article turns anything into a noun

body.p: The neuter article **το** can stand before any word or phrase to treat it as a noun: an adverb, a verb form, a quoted word, a number, a letter.

ex.el: Μην αφήνεις για το αύριο ό,τι μπορείς να κάνεις σήμερα.
ex.en: Don't leave for tomorrow what you can do today.

ex.el: Το έξι είναι ο τυχερός μου αριθμός.
Το γιατί δεν το ξέρει κανείς.
ex.en: The why of it nobody knows.

body.p: Letters of the alphabet are neuter: **το άλφα, το ωμέγα, το σίγμα**. So are all numbers used as nouns: **το δέκα** "the number ten, a ten (grade)".

sections.title: The article before a whole clause

body.p: At B2 the neuter article starts to appear before whole clauses introduced by **να**, **ότι**, **πως** or a question word. This turns the clause into a noun phrase that can be the subject or object of a sentence, or follow a preposition. It is especially common when the clause comes first.

ex.el: Το να μαθαίνεις μια γλώσσα στην ενήλικη ζωή είναι πρόκληση.
ex.en: Learning a language as an adult is a challenge.

ex.el: Το ότι δεν τηλεφώνησε με ανησυχεί.
ex.en: The fact that (s)he didn't phone worries me.

ex.el: Δεν με νοιάζει το τι θα πουν.
ex.en: I don't care what they'll say.

ex.el: Εξαρτάται από το αν θα βρέξει.
ex.en: It depends on whether it rains.

ex.el: Λόγω του ότι ήταν άρρωστος, δεν ήρθε.
ex.en: Because he was ill, he did not come. (formal)

ex.el: Παρά το ότι ήταν κουρασμένη, συνέχισε.
ex.en: Although she was tired, she carried on.

body.p: With a preposition the article is obligatory: you cannot say **από αν** or **παρά ότι**. In formal Greek the genitive appears after learned prepositions: **λόγω του ότι** "due to the fact that", **εκτός του ότι** "apart from the fact that", **πέραν του ότι** "beyond the fact that".

body.tip: In everyday speech the article before ότι is dropped when the clause follows the verb: Ξέρω ότι ήρθε, not Ξέρω το ότι ήρθε. Put **το** in only when the clause comes first, is the subject, or follows a preposition.

check.q: "Whether he comes or not doesn't interest me" begins:
options: Το αν θα έρθει ή όχι...
check.answer: Το αν θα έρθει ή όχι...
check.why: A clause used as a subject at the start of the sentence takes το: Το αν θα έρθει ή όχι δεν με ενδιαφέρει.

check.q: "Apart from the fact that it is expensive" (formal):
check.why: Learned prepositions such as εκτός take the genitive: εκτός του ότι.

sections.title: The article in formal and learned Greek

body.p: Formal Greek keeps several older uses of the article that you will meet in newspapers, laws, academic writing and speeches.

**1. Genitive article with learned prepositions:** **κατά τη διάρκεια** "during", **λόγω της κακοκαιρίας** "because of the bad weather", **εντός της προθεσμίας** "within the deadline", **υπέρ του νόμου** "in favour of the law", **μετά την ψήφιση** "after the vote" (accusative), **ενώπιον του δικαστηρίου** "before the court".
**2. The particles μεν and δε with the article, meaning "some ... others" or "the one ... the other":**

ex.el: Οι μεν υποστηρίζουν τη μεταρρύθμιση, οι δε την απορρίπτουν.
ex.en: Some support the reform, others reject it.

ex.el: Το μεν σχέδιο είναι φιλόδοξο, ο δε προϋπολογισμός περιορισμένος.
ex.en: The plan is ambitious, but the budget is limited.

body.p: **3. Archaic dative forms in fixed phrases:** **τω καιρώ εκείνω** "at that time", **τοις μετρητοίς** "in cash", **εν τω μεταξύ** "meanwhile", **επί τη ευκαιρία** "on the occasion of", **τοις εκατό** "per cent" (written %). These are frozen; do not build new datives.

ex.el: Η ανεργία έφτασε το δεκαπέντε τοις εκατό.

ex.en: On the occasion of the anniversary.

body.p: **4. Article plus participle**, a compact formal way of saying "the person who" or "the thing that":

**5. Article with an adverb or prepositional phrase in nominal style:** **οι τότε κυβερνήσεις** "the governments of that time", **οι εκτός Ελλάδας Έλληνες** "Greeks outside Greece", **οι κατά τόπους αρχές** "the local authorities", **η μέχρι τώρα πορεία** "the course so far".

check.q: Μετά τη λήξη της συνεδρίασης is formal for:
check.why: Μετά + article + noun is the nominal style for "after the end of the session".

check.q: "Paid in cash" (fixed phrase):
check.why: A frozen dative: τοις μετρητοίς. (Πλήρωσε με μετρητά is the everyday alternative.)

body.p: **Article with names in writing and speech.** In biographies, academic prose and journalism, surnames of well-known people often appear without the article in headlines and lists: **Σεφέρης, Ελύτης, Καβάφης**. In running prose the article returns: ο Σεφέρης έγραψε... Leaving it out in conversation sounds cold or bureaucratic.

**The article as a marker of familiarity.** In speech, names with the article and the indefinite article can show attitude: **ένας Κώστας** "some Kostas or other", **ο Κώστας μας** "our Kostas" (affectionate).

**Generic singular.** Formal Greek can use the definite singular for a whole class, as English does in "The wolf is a predator": **Ο λύκος είναι σαρκοφάγο ζώο**, **Ο σύγχρονος άνθρωπος ζει βιαστικά** "Modern man lives in a hurry".
**Omission in headlines and slogans.** Newspaper headlines often drop articles to save space: **Σεισμός 5,2 Ρίχτερ στην Κρήτη**, **Νέα μέτρα για τα ενοίκια**. Don't copy this into an essay.

**Article before οποίος.** The relative **ο οποίος, η οποία, το οποίο** always has the article, which declines with it: **ο φίλος με τον οποίο μίλησα** "the friend with whom I spoke", **η πόλη της οποίας τα σπίτια** "the city whose houses". See the document on pronouns.

**Article and emphasis on quantity.** **Τα πολλά** means "most of it, a lot": Δεν θέλω τα πολλά "I don't want too much fuss". **Τα λίγα** "the little": Με τα λίγα που ξέρω "with the little I know". **Οι περισσότεροι** "most people", **το πολύ** "at most", **το λιγότερο** "at least".

ex.el: Θα αργήσω το πολύ μισή ώρα.
ex.en: I'll be half an hour late at most.

ex.el: Οι περισσότεροι Έλληνες ζουν σε πόλεις.

ex.en: Enough talk. (literally: leave the many words)

check.q: Οι περισσότεροι συμφώνησαν means:
check.why: Article + περισσότεροι = "most".

check.q: Θα κάνει το πολύ τρεις μέρες means:
check.why: Το πολύ is "at most"; το λιγότερο is "at least".

title: The article
blurb: The small word that carries gender, number and case for the whole noun phrase.

intro.p: In Greek the article does far more than say "the" or "a". It is the clearest signal of a noun's **gender, number and case**, often clearer than the noun's own ending, so learning to read and produce the article fast is the shortest route to fluent declension. Greek also uses the definite article in many places English does not (with names, abstract nouns, possessives and whole classes of things), and leaves out the indefinite article in places English needs "a".
This document starts with the forms, moves through the everyday uses, and ends with the article as a tool for turning whole clauses into nouns, which is a hallmark of written and formal Greek.
